newsitem.title: USA: US Commerce allows export of stronger encryption.
newsitem.headline: US Commerce allows export of stronger encryption.

text.p: U.S. Department of Commerce said Friday it granted the first licenses under a new export policy on encryption to three unnamed companies.

The three companies will be allowed to offer products abroad containing 56-bit strength encryption even though the products do not contain "key recovery" features to allow the government to access the keys if necessary.

Until this year, U.S. companies could export products of up to 40-bit strength. Under a new Clinton administration policy, a company can get permission to export 56-bit products if it agrees to incorporate key recovery within two years.
The new policy, which took effect Jan. 1, maintains the ban on export of encryption stronger than 56-bit for products that do not include key recovery.
Many in the computer industry have criticized the administration's new policy as not going far enough to lift the Cold War era export limits that previously treated encryption products as munitions.
William Reinsch, Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration, said in an interview he hoped that the quick action on the three license applications would help quell some of the controversy.

"The only way we're going to convince people in the private sector how we intend to operate this thing is to actually make some decisions, get them out there and let them see," Reinsch said. "I'm happy that we've been able to do this within the first month without rancor or difficulty."

The three companies filed applications within two weeks of the new policy going into effect, Reinsch said. The applications, explaining how the companies planned to incorporate key recovery features into future products, "didn't go into a lot of detail," consisting of four or five page letters with some attachments, he said.
Encryption, computer programs that encode information and render it unreadable without a password or software "key," was once the realm of spies and generals.

But with the explosion of online commerce on the Internet, encryption has become a vital tool for protecting everything from a business' email message to a consumer's credit card number sent over the net.

The amount of protection afforded by encryption is largely a function of the length of the software key measured in bits, the smallest unit of computer data. Companies said products with just 40-bit keys, the old limit, were too easy to crack.
On Tuesday, a University of California graduate student announced he had cracked a message encrypted with a 40-bit key in less than four hours using advanced computers.
Companies have said they see little demand for "key recovery" features and would like to incorporate 128-bit and even longer key lengthes into their products immediately.

But a number of companies, including International Business Machines Corp, Hewlett-Packard Co and Trusted Information Systems Inc, have announced products designed to comply with the current "key recovery" policy.
